facts: It has the longest nave of any Gothic cathedral in Europe.
Jane Austen is buried inside, in the north aisle of the nave.
Winchester was the ancient capital of Wessex and, briefly, of England under King Alfred.
It has the tallest church spire in the UK, at 123 metres.
The cathedral houses one of the four surviving original copies of Magna Carta.
Its clock, dating from around 1386, is one of the oldest working mechanical clocks in the world.
It is home to HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar.
The Mary Rose, Henry VIII's warship, is displayed here after being raised from the Solent in 1982.
Portsmouth Harbour station sits right next to the dockyard and the Isle of Wight ferry terminal.
The palace was originally built for Cardinal Wolsey before Henry VIII took it over in 1529.
It is famous for its hedge maze, planted in the 1690s.
Hampton Court station is the terminus of a short branch line from Surbiton.
The Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew hold one of the largest plant collections in the world.
Its Palm House, completed in 1848, is a pioneering Victorian glass-and-iron structure.
Kew Bridge station is on the south bank of the Thames, a short walk across the river from the gardens.
It is the home of English rugby union and the largest dedicated rugby stadium in the world.
The ground has hosted Test matches since 1910.
It is often nicknamed 'HQ' by English rugby fans.
Richmond Park is the largest of London's Royal Parks, at over 2,500 acres.
It has held a wild herd of red and fallow deer since the 17th century.
The park offers a protected view of St Paul's Cathedral over 10 miles away.
It is the longest parish church in England.
The priory has stood on the site since Norman times, with the current building begun around 1094.
Christchurch sits at the meeting point of the Rivers Avon and Stour.
Poole Harbour is one of the largest natural harbours in the world.
Brownsea Island, where the first Scout camp was held in 1907, sits within the harbour.
Poole's quayside developed as a major trading port from medieval times.
Chesil Beach is an 18-mile shingle barrier beach, one of three major shingle structures in Britain.
It links the mainland to the Isle of Portland.
Weymouth station is the terminus of the line from Southampton and Bournemouth.
Windsor Great Park covers over 5,000 acres and has been royal land since Norman times.
The Long Walk, a 2.65-mile avenue, connects the park to Windsor Castle.
Windsor & Eton Riverside is the historic terminus built for Queen Victoria, closer to the castle's south side.
Guildford Castle's keep dates from the 12th century and was once used as a royal residence.
The castle grounds are now a public garden overlooking the town.
Guildford is the county town of Surrey.
Southampton retains one of the most complete sets of medieval town walls in England.
The Titanic departed from Southampton docks on her maiden voyage in 1912.
Southampton Central is the largest station on the South Western main line outside London.
Osborne House was Queen Victoria and Prince Albert's seaside retreat on the Isle of Wight.
Victoria died at Osborne House in 1901.
Ryde Esplanade connects to the house via a short bus link from the Isle of Wight's rail network.

landmark: Sandown Beach & the Isle of Wight coast
facts: Sandown is one of the Isle of Wight's principal seaside resorts.
The Isle of Wight rail line uses former London Underground trains, replaced in 2021 with refurbished ex-Underground D78 stock.
Sandown's Dinosaur Isle museum reflects the area's rich fossil-bearing cliffs.
Shanklin Chine is a wooded ravine leading down to the seafront, opened to visitors since 1817.
It was used to train commandos for the D-Day PLUTO pipeline operation during the Second World War.
Shanklin is the southern terminus of the Isle of Wight's remaining rail line.
The New Forest was declared a royal hunting ground by William the Conqueror in 1079.
It is still home to free-roaming ponies managed by the New Forest commoners.
Ashurst New Forest station sits right on the edge of the forest's open heathland.
The museum holds one of the world's finest collections of historic cars and motorcycles.
It sits within the grounds of Beaulieu Abbey, on the Montagu family estate.
Beaulieu Road station itself is a remote New Forest halt, with the museum reached by road.
Brockenhurst is the largest village within the New Forest.
Free-roaming ponies are a common sight wandering through the village itself.
Brockenhurst is a key interchange for branch trains towards Lymington.
Lymington's cobbled High Street retains much of its Georgian character.
The town has long been a centre for yachting on the Solent.
Lymington Pier station connects directly to the Isle of Wight ferry to Yarmouth.
Bournemouth's seven miles of sandy beach are among the most visited in England.
The town only developed after 1810, making it young by English seaside-resort standards.
Bournemouth station sits about a mile inland from the seafront, in a wooded cutting.
Milestones is a large indoor museum recreating Hampshire's streets from the Victorian era to the 1930s.
Basingstoke grew rapidly in the 1960s as a London 'overspill' new town.
The station is a major interchange between South Western Railway and GWR/CrossCountry services.
Farnham Castle was built in the 12th century as the residence of the Bishops of Winchester.
The town's Georgian streetscape is considered one of the best-preserved in England.
Farnham sits close to the Surrey/Hampshire border.
Jane Austen's House Museum is a short distance from Alton, in the village of Chawton.
Alton is also the northern terminus of the heritage Watercress Line steam railway.
The town takes its name from an Old English word meaning 'settlement by a source of a river'.
The Devil's Punch Bowl is a large natural amphitheatre of heathland near Haslemere, formed by erosion.
Composer Edward Elgar once lived near Haslemere and was inspired by the surrounding landscape.
Haslemere sits right on the Surrey/West Sussex/Hampshire boundary.
Petersfield's Physic Garden is a recreated 18th-century town garden behind a historic house.
The town's central square retains a bronze equestrian statue of William III, erected in 1757.
Petersfield sits at the northern edge of the South Downs National Park.
Havant is a common access point for walkers joining the South Downs Way long-distance trail.
The town was historically known for parchment and glove-making.
Havant is a key junction where lines to Portsmouth, Chichester and London converge.
Fareham sits at the head of Portsmouth Harbour's Fareham Creek.
The town was historically known for brickmaking, supplying bricks used across southern England.
Fareham is a key junction on lines between Southampton, Portsmouth and Eastleigh.
Eastleigh grew from a small hamlet into a town almost entirely because of its railway works, opened in 1891.
The works built and maintained locomotives for the London and South Western Railway and its successors.
Eastleigh remains a key railway junction on the South Western main line today.
Romsey Abbey is one of the most complete Norman churches in England, founded around 907 AD.
Lord Mountbatten, a former Viceroy of India, is buried in the abbey.
Romsey's Broadlands estate, nearby, was the Mountbatten family home.

landmark: Andover's Finkley Down Farm & Roman heritage
facts: Andover sits near the Roman town of Leucomagus, whose remains lie just outside the modern town.
The Museum of the Iron Age in Andover displays finds from the nearby Danebury hillfort.
Andover is a key junction for lines towards Salisbury and Basingstoke.
Sherborne has two castles: the ruined 12th-century Old Castle and the Tudor 'New Castle' built by Sir Walter Raleigh.
Sherborne Abbey, in the town centre, has one of the finest fan-vaulted ceilings in the world.
The town is often used as a filming location for its well-preserved historic streets.

landmark: Yeovil Junction & the Fleet Air Arm Museum
facts: Yeovil Junction is the mainline station for Yeovil, a couple of miles outside the town centre.
The nearby Fleet Air Arm Museum holds a Concorde alongside its naval aviation collection.
A heritage branch line once linked Yeovil Junction directly into the town, now preserved in part as a walking trail.
Axminster gave its name to a style of woven carpet first produced in the town from 1755.
Axminster Carpets still manufactures in the town today, on a different site from the original works.
The station sits on the Salisbury to Exeter line, run by South Western Railway.
Honiton has been associated with fine bobbin lace-making since the 16th century.
Honiton lace was used for Queen Victoria's wedding dress in 1840.
The town's wide main street reflects its history as a coaching stop on the old London to Exeter road.
The distinctive stepped building beside Vauxhall station is the headquarters of the Secret Intelligence Service, MI6.
Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens, a famous 18th-century entertainment venue, once stood nearby.
The area's name is thought to derive from a medieval manor house, Fulk's Hall.
Kingston upon Thames was the site of Anglo-Saxon royal coronations; a Coronation Stone is displayed in the town.
It has held a market charter since 1200.
Kingston station sits on a loop line served by South Western Railway.
Surbiton's station, opened in 1937, is one of the best-known examples of Art Deco railway architecture in Britain.
Its tall clock tower became an emblem of the modernised Southern Railway of the 1930s.
The station was designed by James Robb Scott.
Brooklands, near Weybridge, was the world's first purpose-built motor racing circuit, opened in 1907.
It was also an early centre of British aviation manufacturing.
The Brooklands Museum now preserves parts of the original banked circuit.
Painshill is an 18th-century landscape garden with follies including a Gothic tower and a crystal grotto.
It was created by the Hon. Charles Hamilton from 1738 onwards.
The station serves both Cobham and the neighbouring village of Stoke d'Abernon.
The London Stone at Staines once marked the western limit of the City of London's jurisdiction over the Thames.
Staines was renamed Staines-upon-Thames in 2012 to emphasise its riverside setting.
The town sits close to the M25 and Heathrow Airport.
Virginia Water lake is an artificial lake created in the 1750s within Windsor Great Park.
The Valley Gardens beside it are known for their spring rhododendron and azalea displays.
A ruined Roman-style temple folly, built from genuine Roman-era columns, stands on the lakeshore.
The Look Out is a science discovery centre set within Swinley Forest, just outside Bracknell.
Bracknell was designated a post-war New Town in 1949 to house London overspill population.
The town's station was rebuilt as part of a major town-centre regeneration.

landmark: Woking's mosque and H.G. Wells connections
facts: The Shah Jahan Mosque in Woking, built in 1889, was the first purpose-built mosque in Britain.
Author H.G. Wells lived in Woking while writing The War of the Worlds, setting the Martian landings nearby.
A tripod sculpture in the town centre commemorates the novel's connection to Woking.
The theme park grew out of Chessington Zoo, which opened on the site in 1931.
Chessington South is the southern terminus of a branch line built specifically to serve the growing suburb.
The park combines a zoo and rollercoaster rides on the same site.
Sandown Park has hosted horse racing since 1875 and was the first course to charge admission to its enclosures.
Esher station has its own dedicated racecourse platform used on race days.
The area was historically part of the Crown estate of Sandown.
Portchester Castle has the most complete Roman fort walls in northern Europe, later built into a medieval castle.
Cosham station is the nearest railhead to both Portchester Castle and Portsdown Hill.
Portsdown Hill above Cosham offers panoramic views across Portsmouth Harbour.
Botley's Market Square still hosts a Friday market, a tradition going back centuries.
The essayist William Cobbett once called Botley 'the most delightful village in the world'.
The village sits on the Hamble River, a tributary of Southampton Water.
Micheldever station sits deep in rolling Hampshire chalk downland, some distance from the village itself.
The surrounding area is part of a large managed woodland, Micheldever Wood.
It is one of the more remote stops on the South Western main line between Basingstoke and Winchester.

landmark: Overton & the Bank of England's paper mill
facts: Overton is home to a paper mill that has produced banknote paper for the Bank of England.
The village sits on the River Test, renowned for chalk-stream fly fishing.
Overton is one of the smallest stops on the line between Basingstoke and Salisbury.
The London Eye opened in 2000 and was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world at the time.
Waterloo is the busiest station in the UK by passenger entries and exits.
The South Bank riverside walk from Waterloo passes the Royal Festival Hall, the National Theatre and Tate Modern.
Battersea Power Station, decommissioned in 1983, was converted into a shopping, dining and residential district that reopened in 2022.
Its four iconic chimneys appeared on the cover of Pink Floyd's 1977 album Animals.
Clapham Junction is the busiest railway station in Europe by number of trains passing through.
